newsitem.title: JAPAN: Asia Metals--Inco woes seen limiting nickel fall.
newsitem.headline: Asia Metals--Inco woes seen limiting nickel fall.

text.p: A possible strike at Canada's nickel giant Inco Ltd's Ontario operations is likely to limit steep falls in nickel, but the metal remains downward biased in the near term, traders said on Monday.
"Nickel might fall further towards $7,230 (per tonne), the latest low where buying by end-users turned the trend," said a trader at a major trading house.
"Yet I'm not too bearish because it's still uncertain what's going to happen with Inco possibly going on strike."

Traders agreed nickel was expected to slide further towards the next support at $7,100 per tonne after spiralling lower in London on Tuesday, breaching successive layers of support on disappointed liquidation and technical selling.
They said the tumble was speculative and was not backed by a change in fundamentals.
Further falls in the metal are likely to be limited by the possible strike by Inco, they said.

Inco's Ontario workers have voted in favour of giving union leaders a mandate to strike if a tentative agreement cannot be reached by May 31 when the current contract between Inco and 4,700 workers expires.
The talks reached an impasse on Saturday.

Traders also expressed concern about news about Sumitomo Metal Industries Ltd's decision to reduce stainless steel output by 10 percent in the April-June quarter in an attempt to boost domestic market prices by July at earliest.
"Now I'm worried about news on Sumitomo. If other (stainless steel) firms follow suit, it will have quite an impact in the market," one nickel trader said.
A Sumitomo Metal spokesman said the company wants to improve profitability following the rising cost of raw materials, such as ferro-nickel.
The bulk of Japan's nickel demand is for stainless steel production. Japan imported 66,667 tonnes of nickel in 1995 which accounted for about 64 percent of its demand.

In the aluminium market, premiums in term contracts with producers for the July-September quarter were being settled at around $86-90 per tonne, reflecting the backdrop of strong global demand, traders said.

"Now we hope we can raise domestic premiums (for end-users) also towards $85-86 (per tonne)," said another trader, adding the premium stood at around $80 before talks with foreign aluminium suppliers began last week.
Japanese traders and end-users had hoped to push third-quarter premiums down to at least $82-85 from current high levels of around $90 in spot deals.
Traders widely expect the country's aluminium demand to fall later this year after surging late last year ahead of the increase in sales tax on April 1.
One trader, however, said: "It's difficult to say at this point, but demand might not decline as much as many fear."
Official statistics released on Tuesday showed April shipments of fabricated aluminium products rose 8.1 percent to a record 225,303 tonnes. It was the 13th monthly rise in a row.
Output of fabricated aluminium also climbed 6.9 percent in April -- the 11th consecutive increase -- to 226,244 tonnes.

Reflecting the strong domestic demand as well as high premiums abroad, aluminium stocks in Yokohama fell further to some 160,000 tonnes at the end of April, well under usual levels of about 230,000 tonnes, traders said.
One aluminium trader added: "It is likely stocks will fall another 10,000 tonnes by the end of May."
The physical copper and zinc market remained very quiet following heavy imports under the Generalised System of Preferences (GSP) scheme in April, traders said.
